note: Tuesday 13 Oct 2026, 07:02 SGT -- before Asia's open (SGX 09:00, HKEX 09:30). Monday 12 Oct's US equity session is now the latest completed close (Columbus Day was a bank holiday for bonds only; NYSE/Nasdaq traded normally). Equities pulled back modestly (S&P -0.06%, Nasdaq -0.44%, Russell -0.45%, VIX +2.49% to 15.21) after Friday's rally, and the gold/silver/miner complex gave back some of Friday's gains too (GLD -0.63%, SLV -0.79%, GDX -0.84%) on dollar strength (DXY an 18-month high, helped by a dovish SNB cut) rather than a break in the safe-haven thesis -- oil extended its rally a THIRD straight session (Brent $106.11 +1.33%, WTI $93.36 +1.64%) on confirmed fresh Hormuz tanker attacks and a Saudi-led ground offensive ("Operation Dawn of Yemen") against the Houthis, with Goldman Sachs raising its December Brent forecast to $90 from $85. The Fed's hawkish chorus firmed further: Cleveland Fed's Hammack said policy should move "relatively quickly" to restrictive, Governor Waller (Oct 8) said he anticipates further hikes if data cooperate, and CME-tracked December cumulative-hike odds rose to ~87% (from ~83% Friday) even as the October-hold probability held near 80-81%. One correction from prior framing: Kevin Warsh is the SITTING Fed Chair (confirmed/sworn in May 2026), not an incoming pick -- his Friday 16 Oct fireside chat with the IMF's Georgieva (Bangkok) is his first public remarks since the September FOMC and will be parsed for tone since he has dropped explicit forward guidance. Credit nuance: CCC/single-B spreads remain wide (~12.5% OAS) and widening, but BB-rated spreads (~194bps) show no stress and some strategists call the move "orderly" -- stress stays concentrated in the lowest credit tier, not broad-based. Rare earths saw a sharp -6% group-wide selloff Monday (MP Materials, USA Rare Earth) on sector sympathy/profit-taking with no company-specific catalyst found, compounding two already-known analyst PT trims (Morgan Stanley, Baird); the Jan 10 2027 China truce-expiry date remains the operative catalyst window.

macro.regime: Hike-biased Fed under Chairman Warsh meets a widening, now ground-offensive Gulf war and credit stress still concentrated at the CCC tier
macro.narrative: The Gulf conflict has moved from strikes-and-rhetoric to an active two-sided campaign: Saudi/Yemeni government forces are conducting "Operation Dawn of Yemen" (launched Oct 5, ~100 aircraft, 300+ targets struck) to retake Sana'a, Houthi strikes on Riyadh/Dammam airports continue, two more tankers were hit near Hormuz Sunday (a Suezmax carrying Iraqi crude among them, two sailors missing), and Trump has still not decided whether the US joins strikes directly -- this is genuine escalation. Oil's third straight gain is a direct, fundamentals-grounded response: Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $90 (from $85), estimating the geopolitical risk premium now adds roughly $20/bbl, while Gulf refined-product exports remain roughly 40% below pre-war levels even as crude exports have partly recovered. On the Fed side, the hawkish chorus firmed further this week -- Cleveland Fed's Hammack (Oct 12) said the Fed should move "relatively quickly" to a restrictive stance given broadening inflation, and Governor Waller (Oct 8) said he "anticipates additional hikes" if data cooperate; December cumulative-hike odds have risen to ~87% from ~83% Friday, with Chairman Warsh's Friday 16 Oct IMF fireside chat the next read on tone. Credit stress is real but more contained than a blanket "cracking" framing implies -- CCC/single-B spreads are wide and widening (~12.5% OAS) while BB-rated spreads (~194bps) show no stress and the move is called "orderly" by some strategists, meaning the risk stays concentrated in the lowest credit tier for now. Gold/silver's Monday pullback and MP Materials' -6% group-wide rare-earth selloff both trace to identifiable, non-thesis-breaking causes (a stronger dollar for metals; sector-wide sympathy selling plus stale analyst PT trims for rare earths) rather than a reversal of either structural thesis.
